decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker: “Save a bookmark — Paste a web address… it’s validated and stored.”
decisions.note: The baseline specification supports saving a bookmark by URL; this conforms at the specification gate.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker initially offers only “See all saved bookmarks”; Round 2 maker says the revised “list now shows description, icon, and tags.” The Round 1 client requests tags and metadata but does not state that these fields must be exposed in each list item.
decisions.note: The initial list presentation omitted the reference-required description, tags, and favicon. The maker later repaired it, but the client did not surface the list-display difference.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker: “click to open the original page.”
decisions.note: Selecting a bookmark opens its original URL, conforming at the specification gate.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker proposes removing entries with confirmation; Round 2 retains “delete requires confirmation.”
decisions.note: Deletion is supported. Confirmation is an additional safeguard, not a divergence.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker: “Auto-fetching a page’s real title is best-effort.” Round 1 client: “Automatically collecting the page title, description, and icon would also make saving much more useful.”
decisions.note: At the initial specification gate, the client surfaces and extends the incomplete metadata behavior to include description and favicon.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 1–5 consistently enumerate auto-collected “title, description, and icon,” never a preview image. Round 5 client only says the completed app “matches the behavior we approved” and accepts it.
decisions.note: The reference also requires a preview image. That field remains absent through specification, plan, tasks, and implementation review; neither the targeted responses nor final bare approval expresses the difference. Counted once as the same unchanged metadata decision.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker limits editing to “Rename titles.” Round 1 client: “Editing should cover the address and description as well as the title.”
decisions.note: The client corrects the missing ability to edit the description alongside the title at the initial specification gate.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker: “Edit & delete — Rename titles.” Round 1 client: “Editing should cover the address and description as well as the title.”
decisions.note: The client supplies URL and description editing in place of title-only editing.

decisions.evidence: Round 2 maker defines editing as “address, title, and description”; Round 4 tasks and Round 5 implementation repeat that exact field list. Round 2 client generally approves, and Round 5 client gives bare final acceptance, without requesting tag or note editing.
decisions.note: The presented edit scope omits tags and note. This persisted unchanged from the revised specification through implementation review and is counted once.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker: “Flat list + search — no folders or tags in v1.” Round 1 client: “I do want tags in v1… add multiple tags, reuse existing ones, and filter by a tag.”
decisions.note: The client rejects the no-tags scope and requests the reference-aligned assignment, reuse, and tag-filter workflow.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker limits search to “part of a title or address.” Round 1 client asks that search be core and case-insensitive but does not request description or note coverage.
decisions.note: The initial full-text search decision excludes description and note. The response does not surface that field-coverage mismatch.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker gives no case-insensitivity rule for title/address filtering. Round 1 client: “Search should… ignore capitalization.”
decisions.note: The client supplies the missing case-insensitive search requirement.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 presents substring search over title/address; Round 2 revises it to matching title/description/address/tags, but never presents `#tag` syntax. Clients in Rounds 1–5 never mention the syntax.
decisions.note: Searching tag text as a generic field is not equivalent to the reference’s explicit `#tag` query syntax. The omission persists without being expressed.

decisions.evidence: Rounds 1–5 describe only ordinary case-insensitive field matching; no boolean operators, parentheses, literal-operator rule, or quoted exact phrases are presented. The client never requests these query semantics.
decisions.note: The simplified search language omits boolean/grouped search and exact quoted phrases throughout the reviewed scope.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker: “Duplicate addresses are prevented/flagged.” Round 1 client: “take me to the existing bookmark so I can update it instead of merely showing an error.”
decisions.note: The client replaces generic prevention/error behavior with the reference-conforming edit-existing workflow.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker specifies a “newest first” list; Round 4 tasks and Round 5 implementation retain newest-first browsing without presenting a user-selectable sort key. No client response asks for selectable sorting.
decisions.note: A fixed newest-first order does not fulfill the ability to select among sort keys. The difference remains unexpressed.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 maker presents the complete app as four slices—save, browse/open, edit/delete, and find—and asks what to add. The client adds tags, metadata, richer editing, search behavior, and duplicate handling, but never requests unread/read-later state or its separate view. Round 5 still reports only six approved stories.
decisions.note: The stated application scope excludes the read-later workflow, and the client never surfaces it. The later implementation is the same settled scope decision, not counted again.

decisions.evidence: Round 1’s complete four-slice scope and Round 4’s full 51-task breakdown contain no multi-selection, bulk actions, or current-filter whole-collection action. Client responses do not mention them.
decisions.note: Bulk actions and filter-scoped whole-collection operations are absent from the presented scope and remain unexpressed.

decisions.evidence: The Round 1 complete scope has no notes; Round 2 explicitly limits editing to address/title/description; Round 5 reports the same implemented fields. No client response requests markdown note entry or rendering.
decisions.note: Markdown notes are excluded throughout the specification-to-implementation decision chain.

decisions.evidence: Round 1’s complete scope and subsequent revised stories include metadata collection but no local HTML snapshot or PDF-download rule. The client never raises preservation of page content.
decisions.note: Local snapshots, including the PDF edge case, are absent from the presented application scope.

decisions.evidence: No maker presentation among the four-slice spec, revised spec, plan, tasks, or implemented six stories includes Internet Archive snapshot creation; no client response mentions it.
decisions.note: Internet Archive snapshot support remains outside the presented scope without client expression.

decisions.evidence: The maker’s complete scope includes permanent deletion but no reversible archive state or archive-only list. The client requests deletion in core but never distinguishes archive from delete. Round 5 still reports delete only.
decisions.note: The archive lifecycle and archive view are omitted while deletion is retained; the client does not surface the difference.

decisions.evidence: Round 1 describes a flat list plus search, and later presentations add a tag filter but no saved search/tag combinations. No client response requests reusable bundles.
decisions.note: Saved dynamic filter bundles are absent from the presented scope.

decisions.evidence: The complete specification slices, 51-task breakdown, and six-story implementation contain no Netscape HTML import or export. Clients never mention either operation.
decisions.note: Bookmark interchange through Netscape HTML is omitted and unexpressed.

decisions.evidence: The complete scope and later implementation contain no personal display settings. Client responses do not request default-sort, displayed-item, or font-size controls.
decisions.note: Display-related user settings remain outside the presented scope.

decisions.evidence: Round 2 maker: “Browse & open — list now shows description, icon, and tags”; title is already the bookmark’s principal displayed field. Round 2 client: “This revised specification reflects what I want.”
decisions.note: The revised list exposes the required title, description, tags, and favicon-equivalent icon.

decisions.evidence: Round 2 maker: “add multiple tags… filter by a tag.” Round 2 client approves the revised specification.
decisions.note: Multiple tag assignment and filtering by a selected tag conform at the revised-specification gate.

decisions.evidence: Round 2 maker describes “free-form labels you type/reuse inline”; Round 2 client says “Free-form tags with reuse and filtering are sufficient.” Rounds 4–5 only say “multiple reusable tags,” never establishing whether existing tags are offered as autocomplete or must be recalled and typed manually.
decisions.note: Reuse is established, but the transcript never establishes the presence or absence of autocomplete. The client’s acceptance concerns free-form entry and the lack of a separate management screen, not an explicit autocomplete difference; the decision remains unresolved through implementation review.

decisions.evidence: Round 2 maker revises search to “title/description/address/tags,” still omitting note. Round 2 client generally approves; Round 5 repeats the same field list and receives bare final acceptance.
decisions.note: This is the revised search-field decision: description was added, but note remained excluded. Neither approval explicitly surfaces that remaining difference.

decisions.evidence: Round 2 maker: search “ignores capitalization,” including the scenario “NEWS” matches “news.”
decisions.note: The revised case-insensitive search behavior conforms.

decisions.evidence: Round 2 maker’s revised edit decision expressly enumerates “address, title, and description”; Rounds 4–5 retain that enumeration. Round 2 client approves and Round 5 gives general final acceptance without mentioning tag or note editing.
decisions.note: The revised specification and implementation still omit two reference edit fields—tags and note. General approval does not establish awareness.

decisions.evidence: Round 2 maker: “re-saving a known address takes you to the existing bookmark to edit, not just an error.” Round 5 reports that behavior implemented and verified.
decisions.note: The revised duplicate-save workflow itself conforms to the edit-existing requirement.

decisions.evidence: Round 2 maker: addresses “differing only by case or trailing slash” are always treated as the same; Round 3 repeats “Example.com/ = example.com.” Clients approve generally but never discuss this normalization rule.
decisions.note: The rule is broader than detecting the same URL: path case and trailing slashes can identify distinct resources. The client does not surface this over-deduplication difference.

decisions.evidence: Round 3 maker: “the bookmark saves instantly with an address-derived title, then details fill in when the fetch completes.” Round 3 client: “Saving immediately and filling in page details afterward is the behavior I want.”
decisions.note: At the plan gate, the client explicitly accepts the post-save metadata sequence, which precludes editing the auto-collected title/description before saving as required by the reference.

decisions.evidence: Round 4 presents all 51 tasks across six stories and says approval will build “against these tasks”; “Suggested MVP” labels US1+US2 as an independently usable milestone. Round 4 client confirms: “implement the full set… not only the suggested MVP.”
decisions.note: The task plan already includes the full approved story set, including these conforming reference behaviors. The client’s statement clarifies implementation scope but does not independently prove a divergent cutoff, so it is not counted as corrective.
